title: The Impact of Popular Artificial Intelligence Tools on English Language Teaching and Learning: A Systematic Literature Review (2021-2025)
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science (IJRISS)
extended_summary:
This paper is not the requested direct secondary study titled "Impact of ChatGPT on the Academic Writing Quality of Senior High School Students" (2024). Instead, it is a broader systematic literature review examining how popular AI tools affected English language teaching and learning between 2021 and 2025. The review asks two main questions: which AI tools were most commonly used in ELT/L, and what impacts those tools had on learner outcomes. It synthesizes prior empirical studies rather than reporting a single intervention on senior high school students’ writing quality.

Using a PRISMA-guided search of Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC, the authors identified 430 records and ultimately included 39 peer-reviewed empirical studies. The review covers multiple categories of AI tools, especially ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, Speech Ace, Google Translate, and virtual assistants. The authors extracted information on study aims, samples, methodologies, tools, and reported effects on writing, speaking, listening, reading, vocabulary, motivation, and teacher workload.

The populations represented across the included studies span higher education, teacher training, elementary learners, and mixed or unspecified K-12 settings across 21 countries. The review notes that much of the evidence comes from higher education and general language learning contexts, with less emphasis on K-12 and low-resource settings. Because this is a review article, it does not provide the intervention specifics, prompts, comparator details, scoring rubrics, psychometrics, or effect sizes for the exact senior-high ChatGPT writing study requested.

The main conclusions are that AI tools show promising benefits for English language teaching and learning, particularly in writing accuracy, vocabulary retention, pronunciation, learner engagement, and reduction of teacher administrative load. However, the authors stress that evidence remains fragmented, with limited longitudinal and experimental work, insufficient reporting on implementation, and ongoing concerns about equity, privacy, overreliance, and teacher preparedness. The paper serves as an evidence map rather than a definitive efficacy study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review using PRISMA-style procedures, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not provide pooled causal estimates. Evidence is synthesized narratively across heterogeneous study designs, so it fits yellow rather than green/blue under the stated framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes broadly positive impacts across literacy, fluency, motivation, and efficiency, but it does not report pooled effect sizes or outcome-specific magnitudes. Because impact is promising yet quantitatively unclear, the most appropriate rating is yellow.

interventions.use_case: Systematic literature review synthesizing multiple AI tools used in English language teaching and learning (e.g., ChatGPT, Grammarly, Duolingo, Speech Ace) across studies rather than evaluating a single intervention directly.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, the paper reports convergent positive effects of AI tools on writing-related outcomes, especially grammatical accuracy, writing enhancement, and idea generation. However, this review does not provide pooled effect sizes, confidence intervals, or harmonized sample totals for the writing outcome specifically; evidence is narrative and aggregated from multiple cited primary studies.
finding.measure: Writing skills, grammatical accuracy, writing enhancement, content generation support

finding.finding_summary: The review reports generally positive impacts of AI tools on speaking, pronunciation, listening, and vocabulary-related language learning, with tools such as Speech Ace, Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, and virtual assistants highlighted for real-time feedback and adaptive practice. No meta-analytic estimates or study-level effect sizes are synthesized, so the magnitude of improvement remains narratively described rather than quantitatively established.
finding.measure: Pronunciation, speaking confidence, listening comprehension, vocabulary retention

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI tools are commonly associated with increased learner motivation, engagement, and autonomy, especially through instant feedback, personalization, and gamified practice. These findings are based on narrative synthesis of included studies rather than pooled statistics, and no standardized effect sizes are reported.

The review identifies concerns that overreliance on AI tools may reduce critical thinking and independent problem-solving, even while some tools may support self-regulated learning and autonomy. Because the discussion is largely cautionary and not supported with synthesized comparative statistics, the net effect on durable skills is mixed and uncertain.

The review reports that AI tools can reduce teacher administrative burden by assisting with grading, feedback, monitoring, and other routine tasks. These efficiency claims are drawn from narrative summaries of included studies and practitioner-focused evidence, with no pooled time-saved metrics or standardized effect estimates reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading support, feedback efficiency, administrative task reduction

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights institutional implications around equitable access, teacher training, ethical governance, privacy, and data security in AI adoption for ELT/L. These are framed as important implementation and policy issues rather than directly measured institutional outcomes, so evidence is conceptually important but empirically limited.
finding.measure: Equity of access, professional development needs, privacy and governance concerns
